title: No Pixel Left Behind: High-Resolution AI-Generated Image Detection
one_liner: Process entire high-resolution images by reading fine details from many local tiles while also seeing the big picture, so forgery signals are not lost to resizing or cropping.
lead: When images get very large, old detection methods chop them up to fit the model, losing tiny telltale marks of AI generation. This paper builds a detector that looks at the entire image at full detail using overlapping tiles, the way a careful crime investigator might scan a whole painting instead of just squinting at the center.

problem.h2: Big pictures reveal lies, but cropping erases proof
paras: A real photograph is just light bouncing off a real thing. An AI-generated image is patterns that a neural network invented, and those invented patterns leave tiny mathematical footprints everywhere—little ripples in brightness that a trained eye (or a trained model) can spot.

When a picture is enormous (4000 by 4000 pixels or bigger), older detection models cannot process the whole thing because they were designed for small inputs. Engineers shrink the image to fit, or cut out just the center. But here is the trap: the fingerprints of AI forgery live in the fine details. Shrinking loses those fingerprints. Cropping chops them off. You end up with a detector that squints at a blurry fragment and guesses.

callout.html: Shrinking or center-cropping high-resolution images erases the fine details where forgery traces hide.

panels.title: 1. Big image, big data
panels.caption: Full image holds many traces of AI forgery at fine pixel scales.

panels.title: 2. Cropping loses half
panels.caption: Old method center-crops, discarding edge regions that hold evidence.

panels.title: 3. Tiling covers it all
panels.caption: New method slices entire image into overlapping tiles at full resolution.

panels.title: 4. Stitch detail + context
panels.viz_args: Local detail tiles + global downsampled view fuse together
panels.caption: Each tile stays crisp; global view prevents local misreads.

panels.title: 5. Forgery signs emerge
panels.caption: Using all pixels lets the detector catch AI fingerprints everywhere.

steps.text: Slice the high-res photo into 16 overlapping rectangular windows, each at full resolution.
Pass each tile into a feature extractor (a pretrained vision model) to capture local patterns.
Also pass the entire image downsampled small into the same feature extractor for context.
Combine the crisp local signals with the global context using learned weighted mixing.
Run the fused features through classifiers to predict fake or real, and locate which pixels look wrong.

paras: The paper moves which pixels are actually processed. Instead of cropping to a tiny window or shrinking the whole image, it ensures every single pixel in the image is read at native resolution. A high-resolution forensic detector sees everything.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Signal-to-noise in fine-detail artifacts
hidden.name: Forgery artifact sharpness
paras: Every forged image carries hidden traces: tiny mathematical inconsistencies in texture, color shifts, frequency-domain patterns that are the fingerprints of AI systems that generate images from text descriptions. A real photo has the noise and randomness of a camera sensor. An AI-generated image has structure that is slightly too smooth or slightly too weird.

The paper measures this by asking: how strong and clear are these fine-grained traces when we process the image at full resolution and full coverage? When you throw away pixels (via cropping) or blur the image (via shrinking), this signal gets buried. When you read every pixel at full detail, the signal shines. The spatial forgery marking module measures which local regions carry the strongest forgery markers, a finer-grained version of the overall prediction.

heat.caption: Darker cells show stronger forgery fingerprints visible at fine resolution.

reads.html: Forgery fingerprints are like ink marks on a forged check. They are everywhere in a fake image, but shrinking or cropping erases them. Detecting them requires seeing the whole picture at full detail.

The paper uses a pretrained vision model backbone to extract features from full-resolution tiles, then applies region-level classification (predicting fake or real for each spatial region) via a trainable refinement layer.

paras: Imagine you have a table cluttered with coins of two different metals. Some are real silver, some are counterfeit alloy. The coins are tiny, so you need good eyesight. If you only look at the center of the table and ignore the edges, you might miss all the fakes that fell to the edges. If you squint from far away (shrink the image), the details blur and you cannot tell the difference anymore.

The paper does something different: it walks to each corner of the table and looks closely at every region, recording what it sees. It also steps back and glances at the whole table to avoid getting confused by one weird corner. Then it stitches all those observations together, weighting the local signals by what makes sense given the big picture. This is why full-resolution tiles plus global context beats any single crop or resize.

stages.s: Slice into overlapping tiles at full resolution
Extract features from each tile and from downsampled whole
Fuse tile features using global context as guide
Classify each region as real or forged

math.words: total_loss = prediction_loss + lambda1 * forgery_localization_loss + lambda2 * quality_estimation_loss
math.equation: L = L_cls(pred, label) + lambda_1 * L_tfl(spatial_forgery_scores) + lambda_2 * L_qfe(estimated_jpeg_quality - true_quality)
symbols: classification loss (how wrong the fake/real prediction is)
ground truth (0 for real, 1 for fake)
token-wise forgery localization loss (fine-grained spatial error)
quality factor estimation loss (how wrong the JPEG quality guess is)
how much to penalize poor localization
how much to penalize wrong compression estimate

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the image is 4000x4000 pixels. Slice it into 16 overlapping 1024x1024 tiles.
Tile 1 (corner): features suggest real with 92% confidence, forgery signal weak.
Tile 5 (center): features suggest fake with 78% confidence, forgery signal strong.
Tile 14 (edge): features suggest fake with 68% confidence, forgery signal medium.
Global view (downsampled whole): context suggests overall 85% likelihood of AI generation.
Fusion step: weight each tile's prediction by its agreement with global signal.
Final output: 79% fake (higher than any single tile because three tiles voted fake and global agrees).
Localization output: spatial heatmap showing which regions carry strong forgery markers (corners+center).
worked.note: The key is that every tile is read at full resolution, not shrunk, so fine details survive.

bars.h2: Full coverage vs. cropping on a large benchmark

charts.title: Old approach: center-crop only
charts.note: Center crop misses forgeries hidden in uncropped regions, dragging accuracy down.

charts.title: HiDA-Net: full-tile coverage
charts.note: Tiles cover entire image, so no forgery fingerprints are lost. Accuracy rises across the board.

items.html: If tiles do not overlap enough, stitching local decisions might create fake seams where tile boundaries meet. The paper handles this by using overlapping regions and fusing via learned weighted mixing, but aggressive non-overlap breaks the method.

If an image is saved with low JPEG quality, compression noise drowns out the fine-grained forgery traces. The QFE module tries to estimate what quality was applied, but if compression is extreme (quality near 0) the signal truly vanishes. The paper shows the method works up to typical compression levels (quality 75 and above) but not extreme compression.

items.b: Images that are both compressed and forged.
items.html: The hardest case: a fake image that was then JPEGed. Compression and forgery both introduce anomalies. The QFE module disentangles them by learning to predict the quality factor, but imperfect estimates can confuse the final prediction.
The method works because tiles are processed at native resolution and fused with global context, so forgery fingerprints remain crisp and visible, unlike cropped or shrunk approaches.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple experiment on a subset of the HiRes-50K benchmark: take ten high-resolution forged images (5 from diffusion models, 5 Midjourney). Implement three detection pipelines: one that center-crops to 512x512, one that shrinks the entire image to 512x512, and one that slices into four overlapping 1024x1024 tiles and fuses them. On each fake image, record where the model's prediction says the forgery is strongest (the spatial heatmap). Measure how many forgery traces each method catches in the uncropped regions.
demo.closing: The tiles-based approach should catch forgeries in edge regions that the center-crop completely misses, proving that full-pixel coverage is necessary for high-resolution detection.
